summary: Specifies the Authentication-Results message header field, which records the results of message authentication efforts so mail filters and mail clients can use them. It obsoletes RFC 7601 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Mail servers check incoming messages for signs of forgery. This document gives them a standard place to write down what they found, in one header field that works for every kind of check. The results are only worth reading if the reader trusts the server that wrote them, so copies that arrive from outside must be removed first.

questions: spf dkim dmarc results in headers
how to read authentication-results spf dkim
subtitle: A standard mail header that records what SPF, DKIM and other checks found about a message.

tldr.problem: Mail servers run checks such as SPF, DKIM and SMTP authentication to judge how much to trust a message, but there was no common place to record what those checks had found, so every scheme ended up inventing its own header field.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines an Authentication-Results header field that a mail server adds at the top of the message. It names the service that did the checking, lists one result per method, such as dkim=pass, and can name the properties that were examined.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8601 replaces RFC 7601 and adds the reverse DNS check called iprev as a method. The field carries no integrity of its own, so receiving servers must strip forged copies and users must switch on its interpretation deliberately.

today: RFC 8601 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 7601, which in turn replaced the original header field defined in RFC 5451, so it is the current definition of the Authentication-Results header field.

sections.title: A Common Place for Authentication Results
sections.content:
The document describes a header field called Authentication-Results that presents the results of a message authentication effort in a machine-readable format. The intent is to create a place to collect such data when message authentication mechanisms are in use, so that a Mail User Agent (MUA) and downstream filters can make filtering decisions or give the user a recommendation about the validity of the message's origin.

End users are not expected to be direct consumers of the field. It is intended for programs that will use the data or render it in a human-usable form. The document specifies the format and discusses the implications of its presence or absence, but not how the data should be used, because that is a local policy and user interface question.

At the time of publication the published email authentication methods are SMTP Service Extension for Authentication, DKIM, DMARC, SPF, reverse IP address name validation, called iprev and defined in Section 3, Require-Recipient-Valid-Since, S/MIME Signature Verification and Vouch By Reference. Author Domain Signing Practices and DomainKeys were previously supported by this framework but have since become obsolete, and the Sender ID specification is no longer supported.

SPF defined a header field called Received-SPF and the historic DomainKeys defined one called DomainKey-Status, but those carry only their own results. The goal of this work is to give current and future authentication schemes a common framework for delivering their results, and to discourage the creation of unique header fields for each.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail servers already run several checks on incoming mail. This document gives them one standard header field where they can write down the outcome of each check, instead of inventing a separate field for every scheme.

sections.title: Trust Boundaries and Who Produces the Field
sections.content:
A transfer from the producer of the header field to the consumer must occur within a context that permits the consumer to treat the producer's assertions as reliable and accurate. The document calls that context the trust boundary of an Administrative Management Domain (ADMD), defined as the delineation between external and internal entities. Services that are internal are provided by the ADMD's infrastructure for its users; services that are external are outside the authority of the ADMD. Hosts inside a trust boundary are subject to the ADMD's authority and policies, independent of their physical placement or operation.

A message can be evaluated inside a trust boundary and then leave it and come back, for example a forwarded message carried as a message/rfc822 attachment or as part of a multipart/digest. The details reported by the field cannot be trusted in that case, so the field is typically ignored in those media types.

The header field often contains no integrity or validation mechanism of its own, so its presence must be trusted implicitly. Valid use therefore requires removing any occurrences of it that claim to be associated with the ADMD when the message enters the ADMD, which ensures that later occurrences were added within the trust boundary. Every field has an authentication service identifier, the authserv-id, which may reference an entire ADMD or a specific validation engine inside it.
sections.plainLanguage: The header field is only worth reading if the reader trusts the server that wrote it. The document therefore draws a boundary around the organisation's own mail system and says that any copy of the field arriving from outside must be deleted before the message is processed inside.

sections.title: The Format of the Header Field
sections.content:
Authentication-Results is a structured header field as defined in Internet Message Format, so all of the related definitions in that document apply. It is added at the top of the message as it transits mail servers that do authentication checks, so that some idea of how far away the checks were done can be inferred. It is therefore considered to be a trace field, and the related definitions apply to it as well.

The value of the header field, after removing comments, consists of an authentication service identifier, an optional version, and then a series of statements and supporting data. The statements take the form method=result and indicate which authentication method or methods were applied and their respective results. For each statement the supporting data can include a reason string and one or more property=value statements showing which message properties were evaluated to reach that conclusion.

The header field can appear more than once in a single message, more than one result can be represented in a single header field, or a combination of these can be applied. The formal grammar is written in Augmented Backus-Naur Form, and Appendix B of the document gives examples of valid header fields with explanations of their semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: The field starts with the name of the checking service, optionally a version number, then a list of results written as method=result, for example dkim=pass. Each result can carry extra notes about which parts of the message were examined.

sections.title: Property Types and Result Codes
sections.content:
Each result is reported with a ptype and a property, which together say where the reported value was extracted from. The initial ptype values are body, for information extracted from the message body, header, for information extracted from the message header, policy, for a local policy mechanism that augments or overrides the result returned by the authentication mechanism, and smtp, for information extracted from an SMTP command used to relay the message. Results reported using unknown ptypes MUST NOT be used in making handling decisions and can safely be ignored.

The policy ptype is special. It says that some local policy was applied that changed the result. A DKIM signature, for example, need not cover the Subject header field, so a receiving domain might decide such a signature is unacceptable even though it verifies, and report the result as policy with a property naming the local check, such as dkim=policy policy.dkim-rules=unsigned-subject.

Each method has its own set of result values. DKIM uses none, pass, fail, policy, neutral, temperror and permerror. SPF uses none, pass, fail, softfail, policy, neutral, temperror and permerror. SMTP authentication uses none, pass, fail, temperror and permerror. The iprev method uses pass, fail, temperror and permerror, and has no none, because every TCP connection that delivers mail has an IP address and some evaluation is therefore always possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Each result can say where the information came from: the message body, the message header, an SMTP command, or a local policy decision. Results that use an unknown source, or that name a method the reader does not support, must be ignored.

sections.title: The iprev Authentication Method
sections.content:
The iprev method checks that a client appears to be valid by looking the client's IP address up in the DNS and finding that the address is explicitly associated with a domain name. The IP address of the client peer is queried for matching names, a number-to-name translation also known as a reverse or PTR record query. Once that result is acquired, a lookup of each of the names, a name-to-number translation or an A or AAAA record query, is done.

Expressed as an algorithm: if the client peer's IP address is I, the list of names to which I maps after a PTR query is the set N, and the union of IP addresses to which each member of N maps after the corresponding A and AAAA queries is L, then the test is successful if I is an element of L. To prevent heavy DNS loads, the number of names evaluated MUST be limited, and Section 4.6.4 of the SPF specification chose a limit of 10 for its implementation of this algorithm.

There is contention about the wisdom and reliability of this test, because arranging for the forward and reverse DNS to match is infrequently observed in some regions. The precise implementation details of a verifier are therefore not specified here. The verifier MAY report a successful or failed iprev test at its discretion, and the document notes that its presence is not an endorsement but an acknowledgment that the method remains common.
sections.plainLanguage: The iprev check asks the DNS two questions about the connecting computer's address: what name points to it, and does that name point back to the same address? The document defines how to report the answer and warns that the check is weak, so it should not be relied on by itself.

sections.title: Adding and Removing the Header Field
sections.content:
A compliant mail server adds the header field after performing one or more message authentication tests, to indicate which server or domain performed the test, which test was applied and what the result was. If more than one test is applied, it adds the field either once per test or once indicating all of the results, and it MUST NOT add a result to an existing header field. It MAY add a field containing only the service identifier and the none token, to say explicitly that no authentication schemes were applied before delivery. The field SHOULD be inserted above any other trace header fields, so that header fields that can be trusted are easy to detect.

To mitigate the impact of forged header fields, any compliant mail server MUST delete any instance of the field that claims, through its service identifier, to have been added within its trust boundary but that did not come directly from another trusted mail server. Each internal server may therefore need a list of the other known trusted servers that are expected to be using the same identifier.

Some sites have a local policy that treats a failure result as a reason to reject the message. In such cases the border server SHOULD issue an SMTP rejection rather than adding the field and letting the message proceed, because a later local rejection can generate a delivery status notification to a forged originator, which is known as backscatter.
sections.plainLanguage: The checking server adds the field at the very top of the message. Every receiving server inside the same organisation must delete any copy that claims to come from inside but did not, so that an outsider cannot forge a passing result.

sections.title: The IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA has registered the header field in the Permanent Message Header Field Names registry, with the IETF as the change controller and the status given as standard.

Three registries hold the tokens used inside the field. The Email Authentication Methods registry records the name of each authentication method together with the properties that accompany its result; an entry has a method, a definition, a ptype, a property, a value, a status of active or deprecated, and a version. No two entries can have the same combination of method, ptype and property. The Email Authentication Property Types registry records the ptype values and what each covers. The Email Authentication Result Names registry records the result codes for each method, and no two entries can have the same combination of method and code.

New entries are assigned only for values that have received Expert Review. This document adds two new DKIM properties, the header.a property holding the value of the signature a tag and the header.s property holding the value of the signature s tag, and it marks the Sender ID and DomainKeys entries as deprecated because those specifications are obsolete.
sections.plainLanguage: Three IANA registries hold the names this header field uses: the authentication methods, the kinds of property, and the result codes. New names are added only after expert review, and retired ones are marked as deprecated.

sections.title: Trusting the Results
sections.content:
A mail server that does not strip forged header fields exposes its users to false conclusions. A malicious user could forge a field using the DNS domain of the receiving organisation as the service identifier and claim the message was properly authenticated. For this reason, processing of the field should not be enabled by default; it should be ignored, at least for filtering decisions, unless specifically enabled by the user or administrator after verifying that the border server is compliant.

Even with forged fields removed, the results can mislead. Until a service for querying the reputation of a sending agent is widely deployed, a pass result does not render the message trustworthy, because spam signed with DKIM by the originator of the spam can pass every check. Mail user agents and downstream filters must take some care with the data even after malicious headers have been scrubbed.

Other points are raised. A verifier that reports an iprev result must not run unbounded numbers of A and PTR queries, because that can be used to attack the DNS. Failing to reject unwanted mail at the border server can result in a denial-of-service attack through generated delivery status notifications, known as backscatter. A compliant installation needs a current list of the internal servers it trusts. Implementers must be robust against intentionally as well as unintentionally malformed header fields. Mail user agents SHOULD ignore instances of the field found inside message/rfc822 attachments, since they are likely to be the results of checks done in the past.
sections.plainLanguage: A passing result does not make a message safe, because spam can be sent from a domain that passes every check. The field can also be forged, so it should be switched on only where the operator has verified that their own servers write it and strip fakes.

viz.caption: The ABNF of the header field, from RFC 8601 Section 2.2

data.title: Authentication-Results grammar
data.code:
authres-payload = [CFWS] authserv-id
             [ CFWS authres-version ]
             ( no-result / 1*resinfo ) [CFWS] CRLF

resinfo = [CFWS] ";" methodspec [ CFWS reasonspec ]
          [ CFWS 1*propspec ]

methodspec = [CFWS] method [CFWS] "=" [CFWS] result

viz.caption: The four property types a result can use

items.title: body
items.text: Information extracted from the body of the message.

items.title: header
items.text: Information extracted from the header of the message.

items.title: policy
items.text: A local policy mechanism augmented or overrode the result.

items.title: smtp
items.text: Information extracted from an SMTP command used to relay the message.

viz.caption: The DKIM result codes, from RFC 8601 Section 2.7.1

items.label: Verified
items.desc: The message was signed, the signatures were acceptable to the ADMD, and they passed verification.

items.label: Verification failed
items.desc: The message was signed and the signatures were acceptable, but they failed the verification tests.

items.label: Not acceptable locally
items.desc: The message was signed, but some aspect of the signature was not acceptable to the ADMD.

items.label: Not processed
items.desc: The signatures contained syntax errors or could not otherwise be processed.

items.label: Temporary error
items.desc: Verification failed for a likely transient reason, such as a temporary inability to retrieve a public key.

items.label: Permanent error
items.desc: Verification failed for an unrecoverable reason, such as a required header field being absent.
